entries.title: Jesse White Tumbling Team eliminated from ‘America’s Got Talent’
entries.summary: <p>The Jesse White Tumbling Team’s journey on Season 21 of “America’s Got Talent” ended on Wednesday night as the Chicago troupe did not advance to the semifinal rounds of the hit reality/competition series. The outcome was revealed during the show’s first results round telecast.</p><p>The team's disappointment was palpable as their hopeful smiles dissolved into heartbreak as the news was announced.</p><p>Viewer votes, based on the previous night’s live quarterfinals performances, determined the three acts (out of 11) that would advance to the next phase of competition — the semifinals scheduled for Sept. 15.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/08/17/jesse-white-tumbling-team-americas-got-talent" target="_blank" >Jesse White Tumbling Team gets second chance on ‘America’s Got Talent’ as troupe rolls into live rounds </a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/6OMWRQEDz1Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Jesse White Tumbling Team Brings the HEAT With 92-Year-Old Jesse White | Quarterfinals | AGT 2026"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Earlier in the evening, the Tumblers were among the top five vote-getting acts overall, which also included Olivia Befus and her trained dog act; rapper Luke Taleno; light-up dance trio Royal Lasers; and comedian Cris Sosa. Befus, Taleno and Royal Lasers earned the round's three spots in the semifinals based on viewer vote totals.</p><p>Four additional “golden buzzer” acts — one from each of the four quarterfinal rounds, and determined by judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Sofia Vergara and Howie Mandel — are automatically propelled to the show's finals on Sept. 22. South Korean magic act Hundred Fingers earned the coveted buzzer on Tuesday night from Mandel.</p><p>The tumblers exhibited their time-tested winning form <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6OMWRQEDz1Q" target="_blank" >during their quarterfinals set </a> on Tuesday night, performing to the pulsating rhythms of Jamiroquai’s “Canned Heat."</p><p>Utilizing two across-stage runs of gymnastic mats, the team flew in and out at a frenetic pace — rolling, jumping, somersaulting and flying through the air, at one point even towering up and over the organization’s 92-year-old founder, Jesse White.</p><p>Cowell praised the performance, commenting: “Well, I loved your first audition, and then I was thinking, Can they make it better on the live shows? Can I be honest? It was better.”</p><p>South Korean K-pop boy band NCT 127 opened the results show on Wednesday night ahead of the group’s upcoming album, "BLINGY," releasing Aug. 24.</p><p>Vergara later took a moment during the telecast to remind viewers of the recent devastating earthquake in Colombia, asking viewers to support UNICEF and World Central Kitchen in their ongoing aid efforts in the region.</p><p>“AGT” fans will be voting for additional semifinalists from three more live quarterfinal rounds airing at 7 p.m. Aug. 25, Sept. 1 and Sept. 8 on NBC.</p><p><i>Miriam Di Nunzio is the former Features Editor of the Chicago Sun-Times.</i></p>
entries.author: Miriam Di Nunzio

entries.title: Court order gives players under pro contracts a chance to return to college sports
entries.summary: <p>Several athletes, including some who signed contracts with NFL teams, were granted a temporary restraining order by a Louisiana court that would make them eligible to return to college athletics, ESPN reported Wednesday.</p><p>Former Oregon State running back Anthony Hankerson (Seattle Seahawks), former Florida and LSU pass rusher Jack Pyburn (Tampa Bay Buccaneers) and ex-Mississippi starters Dae'Quan Wright (Cleveland Browns) and Wydett Williams (Arizona Cardinals) are on NFL rosters and were part of the lawsuit.</p><p>NFL teams are deep into training camp, and rosters have to be cut to 53 players by Aug. 30. Many who don't make those clubs could look for a fallback plan in college football, barring a successful appeal by the NCAA.</p><p>According to ESPN, 16 football players were part of the lawsuit that included 33 athletes across several sports who are seeking a fifth year of eligibility.</p><p>The NCAA has been dealt a series of legal setbacks regarding its eligibility rules.</p><p>"Courts across the country granting relief to ineligible athletes who already had every opportunity to compete in college — sometimes without even having a hearing — are failing to appreciate the destabilizing effect their rulings are having on college sports," Tim Buckley, NCAA senior vice president of external affairs, said in a statement.</p><p>"The lawyers bringing these cases seemingly won't be satisfied until every professional athlete can treat college sports as a fallback option, regardless of the opportunities it strips from those who will never have a chance to begin their collegiate sports experience."</p><p>On July 31, a federal court in Denver ruled that all high school class of 2022 athletes who exhausted their fourth season of college eligibility this spring are eligible for a fifth season this academic year.</p><p>That decision came a little more than a month after the NCAA passed a rule that gives athletes five years to complete five seasons of competition, starting with those who enroll in the fall of 2027. The Colorado ruling eliminated the waiting period.<br></p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Private school advantage? Batavia's Piron, Mount Carmel's Lynch sound off as the IHSA debates changes
entries.summary: <p>Batavia coach Dennis Piron and Mount Carmel coach Jordan Lynch represent opposite ends of the spectrum in the state’s ongoing debate over whether or not private schools currently have an advantage in high school football.</p><p>Their teams matched up in super-charged playoff games over the past several years, and the two rabid fanbases have built a rivalry that might not be entirely healthy. But both coaches are engaging and pleasant and make well-thought out, solid points when they give their opinions on the state’s rules.</p><p>High school sports success tends to have cycles. Private schools are currently riding high on the state’s football scene. The preseason rankings reflect that, as all of the top five schools are Catholic League powers.</p><p>Private schools won all eight of the Class 8A and Class 7A state championships over the past four seasons. Private schools took home 18 of the 25 state titles awarded in Class 4A through 8A since COVID canceled the 2020 season.</p><p>“I’ve been doing this a long time,” Piron said. “The private schools have always been able to attract kids to their schools based on the quality of their programs. I have no problem with that.</p><p>“But in the last 10 years, it feels a little bit more like they are an IMG or a prep school than just a private school. I’ve always thought the Mount Carmel and Loyola’s of the world were tough to beat. And now you have kids announcing things on social media that they are moving from Wisconsin, and you see all the distances they are traveling to private schools. The [private school] coaches are clearly coming out and saying they recruit. That is different.”</p><p>Illinois High School Association rules allow private schools to enroll players within a 30-mile radius.</p><p>Lynch has pointed out multiple times that Mount Carmel’s location actually limits its radius more than 30 miles: “We can’t go in the lake and grab kids.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/19/michael-obrien-preseason-super-25-high-school-football-rankings" >Michael O’Brien’s preseason Super 25 high school football rankings</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/18/mount-carmel-football-chicago-ihsa" >Top-ranked Mount Carmel reloads for five-peat with 19 future college players</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/10/batavia-football-ihsa" >‘Get your popcorn ready’ because it is state title or bust for No. 8 Batavia</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Lynch hasn’t acted differently than private school programs of the past, but he is more willing to advocate for private school recruiting. And he isn’t going to apologize for Mount Carmel’s success. The Caravan have won four consecutive state titles and are heavily favored to win Class 8A again this season. Their roster features 19 players with college scholarship offers. </p><p>“Give the kids and the families some credit, that are traveling within the 30 miles,” Lynch said. “It isn’t easy for them. They have to wake up every Monday, Wednesday, Friday in the offseason and be here at 5:30 a.m. No one sees that; no one talks about that. We have too many critics out there instead of people encouraging these kids and patting them on the back for doing some uncommon things.”</p><p>Mount Carmel doesn’t hide where its players live. The school distributes a media guide which lists the hometowns of every player on the varsity roster. This year’s Caravan is made up of 55 Chicagoans, 17 players from the south suburbs, five players from Indiana and one player each from Skokie, Park Ridge, North Aurora and Lisle.</p><p>“These kids and these parents have a choice,” Lynch said. “For them to pass up a school in their district and come to Mount Carmel and pay tuition speaks volumes. And I think you need to check your own programs. Why are kids passing up your school? They have a choice. They see what is going on here. These kids are pushed every single day. They work hard and we hold them accountable.”</p><p>Boys basketball, the state’s other high-profile sport with a significant fanbase, hasn’t seen such a significant swing towards private school success. Public schools have won 11 titles since COVID with private schools winning nine.</p><p>The IHSA’s competitive balance committee debated the private school dominance issue in mid-July. One proposal discussed creating separate playoff paths for public and private schools, with seven public schools and one private school advancing to the Elite Eight in sports with playoff brackets.</p><p>That’s a drastic step, but certainly better than the prospect of splitting the state tournaments into two, with one for public schools and one for private schools.</p><p>Expect several public schools to propose a change to the 30-mile recruiting radius this winter when the IHSA votes on new bylaws. The issue isn’t going away any time soon.</p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Federal disaster loan centers to open for second time in 2 months following late July storms
entries.summary: <p>For the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/feds-to-open-disaster-loan-application-help-centers-in-wake-of-june-storms" target="_blank" ><u>second time this year</u></a>, the U.S. Small Business Administration plans to open Disaster Loan Outreach Centers for people affected by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" ><u>severe storms</u></a> that ravaged large swaths of Northern Illinois late last month.</p><p>The centers are set to open in Chicago Thursday and in suburban Hazel Crest Friday. The Chicago location will be open until Sept. 3, and the suburban location until Sept. 4.</p><p>They will have representatives to answer questions about the loan program, explain the application process and help to make applications for residents who saw damage from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" ><u>July 27 storms</u></a>. Walk-ins will be accepted, and appointments can be made <a class="Link" href="https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/appointment.sba.gov/__;!!B24N9PvjPQId!Yui7iQbfqrrUKv8IM-98BdLyEdY4caVYvQlLo-hfOfnfkOUBI4UKHY9fTWrFsPblrWUdvM_M9Bs0tZJjcknmMRbMCkoTxQ$" target="_blank" ><u>online</u></a>.</p><p>Homeowners and renters can apply for as much as $100,000 to repair or replace damaged or destroyed personal property like appliances and furniture. Applications are also open for up to $500,000 in low-interest loans to repair or replace real estate damaged or destroyed during the storms.</p><p>Businesses and nonprofits can apply to borrow up to $2 million for damages.</p><p>The deadline to apply for physical property damage is Oct. 19, though economic injury applications aren’t due until May 18, 2027.</p><p>The nearest office and its hours can be found on the U.S. Small Business Administration’s <a class="Link" href="https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/appointment.sba.gov/__;!!B24N9PvjPQId!Yui7iQbfqrrUKv8IM-98BdLyEdY4caVYvQlLo-hfOfnfkOUBI4UKHY9fTWrFsPblrWUdvM_M9Bs0tZJjcknmMRbMCkoTxQ$" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a>.</p><p>The Chicago Public Library’s Pullman branch will serve as the Chicago location. It will be open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Mondays and Wednesdays, noon to 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays and 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.</p><p>The suburban site will be at the Village of Hazel Crest’s building, 3601 W. 183rd St. It will be open 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday, and 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.</p><p>The federal agency <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/feds-to-open-disaster-loan-application-help-centers-in-wake-of-june-storms" target="_blank" ><u>opened outreach centers last month</u></a> following a series of three storms <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/11/obstruction-on-tracks-causes-service-disruption-on-cta-yellow-line-trains-after-storms" target="_blank" ><u>June 10</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/12/chicago-severe-weather-tornadoes-power-outage-comed-customers-englewood" target="_blank" ><u>June 11</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/16/storms-to-bring-torrential-rainfall-potential-flooding-tornadoes-to-chicago-area-wednesday" target="_blank" ><u>June 17</u></a>, which also prompted Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/30/pritzker-disaster-proclamation-tornado-flood" target="_blank" ><u>issue a disaster proclamation</u></a>.</p><p>Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" target="_blank" ><u>signed another disaster proclamation</u></a> Tuesday for the July 27 storms.</p><p>Earlier Wednesday afternoon, the Cook County Board of Review also urged residents to document any damage to their homes that occurred during severe weather this year, as they could <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/19/cook-county-board-of-review-urges-residents-to-start-on-appeals-for-2026-tax-bills-after-recent-storm-damage" target="_blank" ><u>potentially be eligible for reductions on their tax bills</u></a> if the damage meets the county’s qualifications.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/19/cook-county-board-of-review-urges-residents-to-start-on-appeals-for-2026-tax-bills-after-recent-storm-damage" >Cook County Board of Review urges residents to start appeals for 2026 tax bills after recent storm damage</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" >Pritzker signs disaster proclamation to aid recovery after months of ‘relentless and unprecedented’ storms</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Hundreds rally for 'union power' in support of Shedd workers contract fight
entries.summary: <p>Union workers from across the country flooded the lawn outside the Shedd Aquarium Wednesday in support of its union’s fight for a contract.</p><p>Several hundred union members, in town for the national conference of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, chanted and cheered as speakers riled up the crowd demanding Shedd management agree to a contract with better pay and benefits for the Shedd Workers United union.</p><p>Shedd workers moved to form a union in 2024 as part of a larger trend of workers at some of Chicago’s most iconic cultural institutions doing the same.</p><p>Several speakers referenced the fight to be recognized as a union, saying they’ve been fighting for their rights as workers for years as the Shedd has invested in “union busting lawyers” instead of fair wages for union members.</p><p>Union members wore bright green AFSCME shirts and held signs reading “solidarity” and “union power” as chants pulsed through the crowd against the backdrop of the Chicago skyline and Lake Michigan.</p><p>Lee Saunders, president of AFSCME national and Shedd workers, said Shedd's proposals were insulting.</p><p>“They said no, they didn’t want to give you wage increases,” Saunders said. “They didn’t want to give you what you’re due.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> increases for select employees, which he said are “so low they wouldn’t even cover inflation.”</p><p>Shedd worker Nasr bin Safwan took time on the stage to express support for workers at the Art Institute of Chicago, another cultural institution whose union has gained traction in recent years.</p><p>“It's up to us to keep making noise,” he said. “Submit a complaint, write your reviews. When the higher ups don't have our backs, who does?”<br></p>

entries.title: 1 man killed, another critically wounded in McKinley Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>One man was killed and another seriously injured during a shooting in the McKinley Park neighborhood Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The two men, 26 and 56, were inside a van in the 3800 block of South Western Boulevard at 3:51 p.m. when several people got out of a nearby Honda and fired shots, police said. </p><p>The younger man was shot multiple times and taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital where he later died.</p><p>The elder man was shot in the torso and also taken to the same hospital where he was listed in critical condition, police said.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire
